content.text: {"persuasion":"PERSUADED","support_scope":"FULL","rationale":"The book's core identification — the harlot/Babylon the Great of Revelation is unfaithful covenant Jerusalem, the covenant-breaker retaining covenant form without substance — is carried by the cited texts better than the strongest rival (harlot = imperial Rome). Three lines of evidence are decisive on the supplied material. (1) Revelation's own internal cross-reference: 'the great city' of Rev 17:18 is verbally the same designation as Rev 11:8's 'great city, which spiritually is called Sodom and Egypt, where also our Lord was crucified' — an explicit geographic marker that admits only one answer, and the verse itself supplies the hermeneutic ('spiritually is called'), matching the 'MYSTERY' name of 17:5. (2) The covenant logic of the harlot symbol: across the dominant prophetic usage (Hosea 1–3; Ezek 16; 23; Jer 2–3; Isa 1:21 'How is the faithful city become an harlot'), harlotry is defection by a covenanted wife; Rome was never Yahweh's wife, whereas Jerusalem is precisely the city already called Sodom (Isa 1:10; Ezek 16:46), Egypt (Gal 4:25; Ezek 23:19 — the very verse printed with the entry), and the harlot par excellence. (3) The blood criterion: Rev 18:24 ('in her was found the blood of prophets, and of saints') is fixed by Jesus' own words to Jerusalem (Matt 23:35–37; Luke 13:33 'it cannot be that a prophet perish out of Jerusalem'). The Rome reading either splits 'the great city' of Rev 11 from Rev 17–18 without textual warrant, or must absorb the crucifixion locale into 'Roman jurisdiction' at greater interpretive cost. The Rome reading also strains at Rev 17:16, where the beast destroys the whore — self-destruction on the Rome=harlot view, but a natural fit for the beast-power destroying Jerusalem while the woman remains distinct from the seven-headed beast she rides. The book's remaining difficulties (17:9's seven mountains; 17:18's rule over kings) concern the beast she sits on and symbolic scope, and are smaller unsupported steps than the counter's.","book_core_identification":"The harlot ('Babylon the Great, the mother of harlots,' 'that great city') is unfaithful covenant Jerusalem — a covenanted people gone traitor, wearing the form of covenant without its substance, spiritually named Sodom, Egypt, and Babylon.","book_secondary_elaborations":["The Exodus is a scene-for-scene similitude of the Fall of Babylon (plagues, 'come out of her my people,' pursuer sunk like a stone, song of Moses and the Lamb).","Aaron's rod cast down and turned serpent/dragon figures the covenant priesthood gone serpentine, swallowing the nations' dragons and riding the beast.","The geopolitical placement of the last Babylon at 'the hindermost (westernmost) of the nations' via Jeremiah 50:12 and the east-facing Hebrew compass, ridden by the prophet-killing city.","North (tsaphon) as the hidden/lurker's quarter from which the spoiler enters.","The millstone/mountain-cast-into-the-sea phrase-symbol network (Jer 51:63–64; Rev 18:21; Mark 11:23; Rev 8:8) and the 'sink and not rise' vs. baptismal rising contrast.","The forehead name as counterfeit of the seal's inscription and place."],"strongest_counter_interpretation":"The harlot of Revelation 17–18 is the city and empire of Rome: she sits on seven mountains (Rev 17:9, the famous seven hills), she is 'the great city which reigneth over the kings of the earth' (Rev 17:18) — true of Rome, not of first-century Jerusalem — her luxury, global commerce (Rev 18), and persecution of the saints fit imperial Rome, and 1 Peter 5:13 attests 'Babylon' as an early Christian cipher for Rome. This is the dominant historical-critical and patristic reading.","counter_core_identification":"Babylon the Great / the great harlot = imperial Rome (city and empire, with its cult and commerce).","counter_relation_to_book_core":"CONTRADICTS","material_core_denial":"The harlot cannot be Jerusalem because Rev 17:9 places her on Rome's seven hills, Rev 17:18 requires a city with actual dominion over the kings of the earth (Rome, not a Roman provincial city), Rev 18's merchant-and-shipping economy matches Rome's Mediterranean trade, and 1 Peter 5:13 shows 'Babylon' already functioning as code for Rome among the apostles; harlot imagery, moreover, is applied to uncovenanted cities in Isa 23:15–17 (Tyre) and Nahum 3:4 (Nineveh), so the covenant-wife premise does not restrict the referent to Jerusalem.","counter_case":["Rev 17:9 — seven mountains, traditionally the seven hills of Rome.","Rev 17:18 — 'reigneth over the kings of the earth' fits imperial Rome's actual political dominion; Jerusalem ruled no kings.","Rev 18 — the merchants, shipmasters, and luxury cargo catalogue mirrors Rome's commercial empire.","1 Peter 5:13 — 'Babylon' as apostolic code-name for Rome.","Isa 23:15–17 and Nahum 3:4 apply harlot imagery to Tyre and Nineveh, uncovenanted commercial/imperial powers, weakening the claim that only a covenant people can be the harlot.","Broad patristic and modern historical-critical consensus identifies the woman with Rome as persecutor of the church under the emperors."],"book_explanatory_advantages":["Rev 11:8 explicitly names 'the great city' by its crime scene — 'where also our Lord was crucified' — and supplies the 'spiritually called' hermeneutic that matches the MYSTERY-name of 17:5; the identical designation 'the great city' in 17:18/18 binds the passages.","The harlot symbol's dominant prophetic grammar is covenant defection by a wife (Isa 1:21; Hos 1–3; Ezek 16; 23; Jer 2–3); Jerusalem is the canonical harlot, and Ezek 23:19 (printed with the entry) even ties her harlotry to Egypt — one of Rev 11:8's spiritual names.","The Sodom and Egypt names were already applied to Jerusalem by the prophets and apostles (Isa 1:10; Ezek 16:46; Gal 4:25), showing the naming method predates Revelation and points at Jerusalem.","Rev 18:24's blood of prophets and saints is fixed on Jerusalem by Jesus himself (Matt 23:35–37; Luke 13:33), a criterion the text makes identifying.","The woman is distinct from the seven-headed beast she rides; Rev 17:16 (beast destroys the whore) fits the beast-power destroying Jerusalem, whereas harlot=Rome makes the empire burn its own capital.","The 'mother of harlots' fits the covenant order whose daughter-defections learned the trade in her house, and coheres with the wife/bride antithesis (harlot city vs. New Jerusalem the bride)."],"counter_explanatory_advantages":["Rev 17:9's seven mountains map naturally onto Rome's seven hills without any symbolic re-routing.","Rev 17:18's literal dominion 'over the kings of the earth' describes Rome, not Jerusalem; the book must take this symbolically.","Rev 18's maritime commerce catalogue fits Rome's trade empire more naturally than Jerusalem's economy.","1 Peter 5:13 provides independent first-century evidence of 'Babylon' as a cipher for Rome.","Tyre and Nineveh as harlots (Isa 23; Nah 3:4) show the image can attach to uncovenanted imperial powers."],"evidence_book_core_cannot_explain":[],"comparative_winner":"BOOK","decisive_sources":["Revelation 11:8 with Revelation 17:18 — the shared designation 'the great city' plus the explicit crucifixion locale and the 'spiritually called' naming method","Isaiah 1:21 with Ezekiel 16 and 23 (esp. Ezek 23:19) — the harlot as the covenant wife, Jerusalem, including her Egypt-harlotry","Revelation 18:24 with Matthew 23:35–37 and Luke 13:33 — the blood-of-prophets criterion fixed on Jerusalem","Isaiah 1:10; Ezekiel 16:46; Galatians 4:25 — prior prophetic/apostolic precedent for calling Jerusalem Sodom and Egypt","Revelation 17:5 and 17:15–16 — the mystery-name and the woman/beast distinction, with the beast destroying the whore"],"unresolved_objections":["Rev 17:9's seven mountains most naturally evoke Rome's seven hills; the book's relocation of the final Babylon to a westernmost seven-mountain bloc via Jer 50:12 and the qedem compass is speculative and not established by the cited texts.","Rev 17:18's 'reigneth over the kings of the earth' remains more naturally true of Rome; the book's symbolic account (the covenant order gone serpent, swallowing and riding the nations) is a mechanism, not a demonstration.","Isa 23:15–17 (Tyre) and Nah 3:4 (Nineveh) stand as counter-texts to the strong claim that only a covenant people can be called a harlot, though they do not overturn the dominant covenant-wife usage.","1 Peter 5:13's apparent Babylon=Rome cipher is not addressed by the supplied argument.","Rev 18's merchant-and-shipping economy is not obviously Jerusalem's, and the book's transhistorical/end-scale reading of the fall (Exodus similitude 'on every nation at once') is elaboration beyond the core identification."],"confidence":"medium"}
